one_liner: Hand-written PTX flash-attention prefill and paged decode library for RTX 5080 (sm_120); edges out vLLM's FlashAttention-2 at small batch.
what_it_does: A standalone CUDA static library (namespace transformer) for forward attention on consumer GPUs: batched or varlen prefill, causal or full, MHA/GQA/MQA, fp16/bf16, head dim 64 or 128, plus split-KV decode against a paged KV cache with optional FP8 or INT4 quantization and a fused-RoPE cache writer. The API is three C++ callables (fa_attention, fa_cache_attention, fa_cache_write) taking zero-initialized argument structs and a cudaStream_t, mirrored in Python as the fa_ptx PyTorch package (attention, PagedKVCache, CaptureCache for CUDA-graph decode). Varlen layout and bottom-right causal alignment follow vLLM/FA2 conventions, but it is not a drop-in for the flash_attn Python API.
how_it_is_fast: It uses PTX mma.sync.m16n8k16 with ldmatrix and cp.async, the tensor-core path consumer Blackwell has (no WGMMA or TMA), and keeps the whole online softmax in registers. The saturated-grid 'fat-warp' kernel gives each of 4 warps one 16-row Q tile, so softmax needs only intra-warp shuffles, and feeds P straight from the QK accumulator fragment into the PV MMA without touching shared memory; K and V loads are software-pipelined behind the matmuls. An exp2 fold (scale times log2 e folded into the score multiply) makes every exponential a raw EX2, and a runtime dispatcher sends under-saturated grids (B=1, short S) to a 32-row split-N tile that doubles the CTA count, with optional per-shape autotuning cached in a wisdom file.
when_to_use: Causal fp16/bf16 prefill on an RTX 5080-class consumer Blackwell GPU at batch 1 with S up to 2048, where it measured 9-32% lower latency than vLLM 0.23's FA2 at D=64 and 4-17% at D=128 (gains shrink to 0-16% at B=4-8 with S<=1024)
Building a small custom inference loop in C++ or PyTorch on a GeForce card that needs varlen prefill, a paged KV cache and CUDA-graph-captured decode without pulling in vLLM or FlashInfer
Long-context decode where VRAM is tight, using the FP8 KV cache (documented ~1.8x faster decode at D=128 long context, ~0.035 worst-case nrmse)
Studying how to reach ~85% of tensor-pipe peak with mma.sync on sm_120; the docs record each optimization step and the failed experiments
when_not_to_use: Large batch times long context (B>=4 with S>=4096, or Llama-class H=32 at B>=4): it loses to vLLM FA2 by 2-5%
Training: only forward prefill and decode kernels are documented, no backward pass
Hopper or datacenter Blackwell GPUs, where FlashAttention-3 or cuDNN with WGMMA/TMA apply; it builds for sm_80 and up but was tuned and measured only on one RTX 5080
Head dims other than 64 or 128, or quantized prefill: FP8/INT4 caches are decode-only, and INT4 KV collapsed generation quality on Qwen2.5-1.5B (30/64 teacher-forced argmax agreement)
You need a cuDNN comparison or a license file for compliance review: neither exists in the repo (MIT is stated only in the README)

integration.form: static lib (CMake target flash_attention) plus an optional PyTorch CUDAExtension (fa_ptx, pip install -e python/)
integration.dependencies: CUDA runtime only for the C++ library; PyTorch with CUDA and nvcc for the Python bindings
integration.min_toolchain: CUDA Toolkit 12.0+ (tested with 13.1), CMake 3.20+, C++17; Python >= 3.9 for fa_ptx
integration.platforms: NVIDIA compute capability 8.0+ (CMake builds sm_80/86/89/90/120), tuned only for sm_120 RTX 5080; developed on Windows (MSVC flags in setup.py and docs) and benchmarked against vLLM under WSL2
integration.thread_safety: not documented; every call takes an explicit cudaStream_t and the docs say all kernels are deterministic, but concurrent use of autotune and its wisdom file is not covered
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same varlen packing and bottom-right causal convention as vLLM's flash_attn_varlen_func, but a different C++/Python API with its own args structs and cache object

gotchas: Errors terminate the process: bad arguments abort with an 'fa_*:' message and the header's CUDA_CHECK calls exit(EXIT_FAILURE), so wrap it if your host process must survive misuse
Index arrays (cu_seqlens, block_table, seq_lens, slot_mapping) must be device memory; host pointers give garbage output without an abort, per the troubleshooting table
FP8 caches need k_scale/v_scale > 0 set by you (zero-init default aborts); decode needs a scratch buffer sized by fa_cache_attention_scratch_bytes

The default branch is dev/FlashAtt with no tags or releases, the README clone URL is a placeholder (yourusername/flash-attention-cuda), and docs/cutlass-comparison.md still calls the prefill kernel MHA-only while how-to-use.md documents GQA
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over learn-cuda's SM120 attention or Mini-Attention when you need a usable library rather than a teaching kernel: varlen, GQA, paged and quantized KV decode, and torch.compile/CUDA-graph-ready bindings. Pick SageAttention instead if quantized QK is acceptable and you want larger consumer-GPU speedups; learn-cuda's RTX 5090 data puts PyTorch's cuDNN SDPA backend ahead of both its own kernel and the flash-attn FA2 package, and this repo never measured cuDNN.
verified_claims_summary: In a same-process harness on an RTX 5080 (shared torch.randn fp16 inputs, interleaved rounds, outputs cross-checked to ~2e-4 nrmse), causal prefill latency against vLLM 0.23.0's bundled FA2 (flash_attn_varlen_func, driver-JIT from sm_80 PTX) was strictly lower at 17 of 34 shapes; the '23 of 34' headline also counts 6 losses under 2%. Wins concentrate at B=1 and short context (up to +31.9% at B=1, S=1024, D=64); losses reach -4.8% at the largest batch x context shapes; peak is ~202 vs ~212 TFLOPS. The vLLM harness script (fa_sweep2.py) is not in the repo, and the end-to-end Qwen2.5-1.5B decode wins (4.70 vs 5.12 ms/token at B=1, 5.28 vs 5.43 ms at B=8) compare this repo's best-of-3 runs on a Windows desktop GPU (5-15% run-to-run spread) with vLLM's 5-iteration average, including its scheduler and sampler.
status_note: Active single-author project (76 commits, last 2026-07-03, 12 stars) with seven correctness-gate executables; MIT per the README but no LICENSE file, so confirm the license with the author before vendoring.
